description: Choose gravitational softening from the simulator's actual resolution - pixel footprint, patch size, or local cell width - instead of pretending one epsilon works at every zoom level. This borrows anti-aliasing and mesh-resolution logic from graphics and FEM so a minimal simulator degrades honestly when representation gets coarse.
mathematical_formalization: eps_i = max(eps_phys, k_screen * s_px(i), k_cell * h_cell(i)); a_i = sum_j G m_j r_ij / (||r_ij||^2 + eps_ij^2)^(3/2), with eps_ij = max(eps_i, eps_j)
analogical_connections: An anti-aliasing kernel in graphics becomes a force-blur kernel in gravity.
Finite-element mesh size defines what spatial detail is actually resolvable.
Sensor blur suggests admitting when the representation cannot support sharp forces.
implementation_hypothesis: Measure screen-world scale each frame in interactive mode or local cell size in batch mode; set epsilon from that scale; show the effective epsilon as an overlay so users can see when the simulator is intentionally smoothing.
experiment_seed: Run the same scene across repeated zoom-in and zoom-out cycles; compare stability, aliasing, and conservation metrics for fixed epsilon versus scale-aware epsilon.

closest_prior_art.title: REBOUND: An open-source multi-purpose N-body code for collisional dynamics

novelty_claim: The novelty is to bind the smoothing scale to representational limits rather than only to physical heuristics or density estimates.
differentiation: Adaptive softening in self-gravity codes is usually motivated by particle density or kernel support. Here the driver is what the simulator can honestly resolve and display, which is a different control signal.
experimental_result: Invalidated on the star-grazing stress case: no tested dt enters the declared safe regime, and the scale-coupled epsilon distorts the trajectory more than the encounter-microstep branch.
